tracks.title: Electronics Basics
tracks.blurb: No board, no code: what electricity is, how voltage, current and resistance work, and what every common component does, told in pictures and animations.

overview.heading: Electrons on the move
overview.text: Everything is made of atoms, and every atom has electrons. In a metal wire some of them roam free. A battery gives them a push: they drift slowly, but the push itself races along the wire almost instantly.

overview.heading: Push, flow and resistance
overview.text: Voltage is the push that lifts electrons up an energy hill. Current is how many flow past each second. Resistance is how hard the path is. Change one and watch the others respond in a live circuit.

overview.heading: V = I × R
overview.text: Voltage, current and resistance are tied together by one simple rule. Slide the voltage and the resistor, watch the current change, light an LED safely and see why fuses exist.

overview.heading: No loop, no current
overview.text: Current only flows round a complete loop. A switch is a deliberate gap you can open and close. See what a loose wire does, why a short circuit is dangerous, and how a push button differs from a toggle.

overview.heading: One path or many
overview.text: Bulbs in series share one path and share the battery’s push, so they dim. In parallel, each bulb has its own path and stays bright, but the battery has to supply more current. Tap bulbs to unscrew them.

overview.heading: Chemistry that pushes
overview.text: Inside a battery, zinc and manganese dioxide react and push electrons out of the − end. The result is direct current: steady and one way. Stack cells to add voltage, and read mAh to know how long they last.

overview.heading: Read a resistor
overview.text: Resistors are too small to print numbers on, so they wear coloured bands. Two digits, a multiplier and a tolerance. Tap the bands, pick colours and read the value like a pro.

overview.heading: A one-way light
overview.text: A diode lets current through one way only, like a flap valve. An LED is a diode that glows. Put it in the right way round, always with a resistor, and it lasts for years.

overview.heading: A tiny charge store
overview.text: A capacitor stores charge on two plates. Charged through a resistor it fills fast at first, then slower: after one time constant, R × C, it is 63 % full. That curve lets circuits keep time and smooth power.

overview.heading: A small current controls a big one
overview.text: A transistor is a switch with no moving parts. A tiny current into the base lets a current about 100 times bigger flow from collector to emitter. Use it to switch a lamp or amplify a signal.

overview.heading: A knob that divides voltage
overview.text: Inside a potentiometer a wiper slides along a resistor track, splitting it into two parts. That makes a voltage divider: turn the knob and the middle pin goes smoothly from 0 to 5 V, which an Arduino reads as 0 to 1023.

overview.heading: Magnetism makes motion
overview.text: Current makes a magnetic field. Coil the wire and it becomes a magnet that magnets can push, which is how a motor spins. Turn the motor by hand instead and it makes electricity: a generator.

overview.heading: Circuits without solder
overview.text: A breadboard hides metal clips under its holes. Each short column of five holes is one connection, the middle gap separates the halves, and long rails carry power. X-ray it and tap holes to see what joins what.

overview.heading: See the invisible
overview.text: A multimeter turns volts, amps and ohms into numbers. Measure volts across a part, amps with the meter in the loop, ohms with the power off, and listen for the continuity beep.

overview.heading: Make a joint that lasts
overview.text: Soldering joins metal with melted metal. Heat the pad and the leg together, feed in solder, remove the solder then the iron, and leave a shiny cone. Safety first: glasses, fresh air and the iron in its stand.

tracks.title: How Sensors See
tracks.blurb: How machines sense the world: ultrasonic echoes, infrared, radar, lidar, cameras, accelerometers and more, animated step by step.

overview.heading: Seeing with sound
overview.text: An ultrasonic sensor chirps at 40 kHz, far too high for us to hear, and times how long the echo takes to come back. Sound travels at 343 m/s, so distance = time × speed ÷ 2. Drag the wall and watch the echo time change.

overview.heading: Invisible light
overview.text: Infrared is light just beyond red. Obstacle and line sensors shine it and measure what bounces back. TV remotes flash it in quick 38 kHz bursts that spell out a code, so ordinary lamps and sunlight can’t confuse the receiver.

overview.heading: It feels your warmth
overview.text: A PIR sensor sends nothing out. It watches the infrared glow of warm bodies with two side-by-side halves. Its dome splits the room into zones, so walking past makes the halves disagree, and that change triggers the output.

overview.heading: Echoes at light speed
overview.text: Radar sends radio waves and times their echoes. They travel at light speed, so a microsecond there and back means 150 m. If the target moves, the echo’s frequency shifts: the Doppler effect lets a speed gun measure a car.

overview.heading: A map made of dots
overview.text: Lidar fires laser pulses and times their return to the nanosecond. A spinning mirror sweeps the beam around, and each echo becomes a dot. Thousands of dots form a point cloud: a map robots and self-driving cars use to see.

overview.heading: Millions of light buckets
overview.text: A lens focuses the world onto a grid of pixels, each counting light as a number. Pixels can’t see colour, so a mosaic of red, green and blue filters sits on top and the camera fills in the gaps. Exposure trades brightness against blur.

overview.heading: A tiny mass on springs
overview.text: Inside a motion-sensor chip a microscopic mass hangs on springs. Tilt or shake the chip and the mass moves; comb fingers measure the gap. A gyroscope wiggles a mass, and turning nudges it sideways. Phones use both.

overview.heading: Resistance that responds
overview.text: A thermistor’s resistance falls as it warms; a light-dependent resistor’s falls as light rises. Put either one in a voltage divider and the change becomes a voltage an Arduino can read as a number.

overview.heading: Circles in the sky
overview.text: GPS satellites broadcast the exact time from atomic clocks. Your receiver times each signal’s trip to work out distances, and where the distance circles meet, that’s you. A fourth satellite fixes the receiver’s own clock error.

tracks.title: How Computers Think
tracks.blurb: From a switch to a processor: binary, logic gates, memory, the fetch-decode-execute cycle, x86 versus ARM, GPUs and AI accelerators.

overview.heading: Counting with switches
overview.text: Computers store everything as bits: switches that are off (0) or on (1). Eight bits make a byte. Each switch is worth double the one on its right, so a byte can count from 0 to 255, and letters are just numbers too.

overview.heading: Decisions from switches
overview.text: A transistor is a switch flipped by electricity. Wire switches in a row and you get AND; side by side, OR; one that shorts the output, NOT. Combine them and you can build any decision a computer makes.

overview.heading: Maths made of logic
overview.text: In binary, 1 + 1 = 10: write 0, carry 1. A half adder is just an XOR (sum) and an AND (carry). Add a carry input and chain four of them, and you can add two 4-bit numbers as the carry ripples across.

overview.heading: Circuits that remember
overview.text: A button forgets the moment you let go. Two NOR gates feeding each other make a latch that remembers one bit. Line up eight for a byte, give each byte an address, and you have RAM you can write to and read back.

overview.heading: The heartbeat of a chip
overview.text: A quartz crystal vibrates at an exact rate and makes a clock signal: high, low, high, low. On each rising edge every part of the processor takes one step together. An Uno ticks 16 million times a second; a laptop, billions.

overview.heading: Inside a tiny CPU
overview.text: A processor repeats three steps forever: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it. Step through a tiny 8-instruction CPU with a program counter, instruction register, control unit, ALU and A register.

overview.heading: One chip, or a whole system
overview.text: A microcontroller puts processor, memory and pins on one chip: it runs one program, starts instantly and sips power. A microprocessor is just the brain, with memory, storage and more outside, so it can run a full operating system.

overview.heading: Two instruction languages
overview.text: Intel and AMD chips speak x86: many instructions, 1 to 15 bytes long. Phones speak ARM: simpler, fixed 4-byte instructions. Both pipeline work like a factory line. Phones add big and little cores and pack everything into one system-on-chip.

overview.heading: Many hands make light work
overview.text: A CPU has a few fast, clever cores. A GPU has thousands of simpler ones that all do the same sum on different data at once. Race them colouring pixels, then meet the 1024 CUDA cores on a Jetson Orin Nano.

overview.heading: Multiply, add, repeat
overview.text: A neural network is layers of neurons that multiply inputs by weights, add them up and light up if the total is positive. A whole layer is one matrix multiply, and AI chips are grids of multiply-add units doing trillions a second.

tracks.title: Arduino Foundations
tracks.blurb: Your first circuits on an Arduino-style board: LEDs, buttons, knobs, sound, motors, timing and your first complete project.

overview.heading: An Uno-style board
overview.text: This is the most popular board for learning electronics. A small microcontroller reads inputs (buttons, sensors) and controls outputs (lights, motors, sound) by running a program called a sketch.

overview.heading: Blink an LED
overview.text: Your first real circuit: an LED and a resistor on a breadboard, driven by pin 13. Switching the pin on and off with a pause in between makes it blink.

overview.heading: Push a button
overview.text: Inputs let the board sense the world. A push button connects pin 2 to ground when pressed. With the built-in pull-up resistor, the pin reads HIGH when released and LOW when pressed.

overview.heading: Turn a knob
overview.text: A potentiometer is a resistor with a sliding contact. Its middle pin outputs a voltage between 0 and 5 V depending on where the knob is, and analogRead() turns that into a number.

overview.heading: Mix colours
overview.text: An RGB LED hides a red, a green and a blue LED inside one lens, sharing a common ground. Set each one’s brightness with PWM and the light blends into any colour you like.

overview.heading: Sense light
overview.text: A light-dependent resistor (LDR) conducts better the more light falls on it. Paired with a fixed resistor it makes a voltage divider, so the voltage on A0 rises in bright light and falls in the dark.

overview.heading: Make a sound
overview.text: A piezo buzzer clicks every time its pin changes. Flip the pin 440 times a second and you hear the note A. The tone() function does the flipping for you in the background.

overview.heading: Control a motor
overview.text: A pin can only supply about 20 mA — far too little for a motor. Instead, the pin drives an NPN transistor, which switches the motor’s much larger current from the 5 V supply.

overview.heading: Sense heat
overview.text: The TMP36 turns temperature into a voltage: 0.5 V at 0 °C, plus 10 mV for every degree. A little maths converts the analogRead() value back into degrees.

overview.heading: Sweep a servo
overview.text: A servo is a motor that knows where it is. Send it a pulse between 1 and 2 ms long and it turns to a matching angle between 0° and 180° — and holds it there. The Servo library handles the pulses.

overview.heading: Read a sensor
overview.text: The HC-SR04 sends out a burst of ultrasound and listens for the echo, like a bat. Sound travels about 0.0343 cm per microsecond, so timing the round trip tells you the distance.

overview.heading: Traffic lights
overview.text: Three LEDs, three pins and a fixed sequence: red, red + amber, green, amber, back to red. A small helper function sets all three lights at once, so loop() reads like the timetable of a real junction.

overview.heading: Fade an LED
overview.text: A digital pin can only be fully on or off — but switch it fast enough and your eye averages the pulses. analogWrite() sets the share of time the pin is on (the duty cycle), and two for loops sweep it up and down so the LED breathes.

overview.heading: LED chaser
overview.text: Six LEDs light one after another and bounce back, like the scanner on a sci-fi car. Instead of six copies of the same code, the pin numbers live in an array and a for loop walks through it.

overview.heading: Talk to your board
overview.text: Serial works both ways. Type a command in the serial monitor and the board reads it as a String, cleans it up with trim() and decides what to do. It’s the simplest user interface there is — and a superb debugging tool.

overview.heading: Toggle with a button
overview.text: A light switch, not a doorbell: press once for on, again for off. The trick is to react to the moment the button goes down (an edge), remember the LED’s state in a variable, and ignore the few milliseconds of contact bounce with millis().

overview.heading: Multitask with millis()
overview.text: delay() stops everything. Instead, check the clock: millis() counts milliseconds since power-up, and each task asks “has enough time passed since I last ran?”. Loop spins thousands of times a second, so two blinkers and a button all run at once.

overview.heading: Build a project
overview.text: Put it all together: the distance sensor watches the car and a traffic light tells the driver when to stop. This is a real parking assistant built from parts you already know.

tracks.title: Sensors & Inputs
tracks.blurb: Let your projects sense the world: motion, temperature, humidity, sound, gas, flame, touch, tilt, remotes and keypads.

overview.heading: Motion alarm
overview.text: A PIR (passive infrared) sensor sees the heat your body gives off. When a warm shape moves across its view, the module pulls its OUT pin HIGH for a few seconds. The sketch just reads that pin like a button and sounds the alarm.

overview.heading: Temperature & humidity
overview.text: The DHT11 measures temperature and relative humidity and sends both down a single data wire in a timed pulse code. The DHT library decodes it, and even works out the heat index — how hot it actually feels.

overview.heading: Thirsty plant
overview.text: A capacitive probe senses how much water is around it: wet soil reads lower, dry soil higher. Every probe is a little different, so you calibrate it — note the reading in dry air and in water — and map() the raw number onto 0–100 %.

overview.heading: Clap switch
overview.text: The sound module’s DO pin pulses HIGH on any loud noise. A single bang shouldn’t switch the lights, so the sketch waits for two claps close together, using millis() timestamps to ignore echoes and claps that are too slow.

overview.heading: Gas leak alarm
overview.text: The MQ-2 has a heated bead of tin oxide whose resistance drops when flammable gas or smoke touches it. Read its voltage with analogRead(), compare it with a threshold and sound an alarm. It needs to warm up first — skip that and you’ll get false alarms.

overview.heading: Flame detector
overview.text: Flames glow brightly in infrared. The sensor’s dark receiver measures that IR and gives you two outputs: AO, the raw level, and DO, a simple yes/no from an on-board comparator. Light the candle, move it around and watch both.

overview.heading: Read a joystick
overview.text: A thumb joystick is two potentiometers at right angles plus a push switch. Read X and Y with analogRead(), the switch with digitalRead(), then steer a servo with the X axis.

overview.heading: Feel the force
overview.text: A force-sensing resistor (FSR) drops from over 1 MΩ to a few hundred ohms as you press it. Paired with a 10 kΩ resistor it forms a voltage divider, so A0 rises with force — enough to dim an LED and sort presses into categories.

overview.heading: Click wheel
overview.text: A rotary encoder turns forever in clicks. Inside, two switches (CLK and DT) open and close slightly out of step — quadrature. Whichever changes first tells you the direction, so you can count up and down.

overview.heading: Sense tilt
overview.text: The MPU-6050 has a 3-axis accelerometer and gyro. At rest, the accelerometer only feels gravity, so the way that 1 g is shared between X, Y and Z tells you how the board is tilted. atan2() turns it into pitch and roll.

overview.heading: Remote control
overview.text: A TV-style remote flashes an infrared LED 38,000 times a second in coded bursts. The receiver strips the 38 kHz carrier, and the IRremote library decodes the bursts into an address and a command byte you can switch on.

overview.heading: Keypad door lock
overview.text: A membrane keypad is a grid of switches: 4 row wires and 4 column wires make 16 keys from 8 pins. The Keypad library scans them for you. Collect four digits, check them on #, and swing a servo bolt open.

tracks.title: Displays, Light & Motion
tracks.blurb: Show information and move things: 7-segment, LCD and OLED displays, NeoPixels, shift registers, steppers, relays and motor drivers.

overview.heading: Count on a 7-segment display
overview.text: A 7-segment display is eight LEDs — bars a to g plus a dot — sharing one common cathode. Store which segments make each digit in a byte, then copy the byte’s bits onto eight pins to count 0–9, or all the way to F in hex.

overview.heading: 8 LEDs from 3 pins
overview.text: The 74HC595 is a shift register: clock in eight bits one after another on a single data pin, then pulse the latch and all eight outputs change together. Three Arduino pins drive eight LEDs — and you can chain more chips for 16, 24…

overview.heading: Character LCD
overview.text: A 16×2 LCD shows two lines of text. The I²C backpack on its back turns 16 fiddly pins into four, and LiquidCrystal_I2C gives you print(), setCursor() and even your own characters.

overview.heading: OLED graphics
overview.text: An SSD1306 OLED has 8,192 pixels that glow on their own. The Adafruit libraries draw text, rectangles and lines into a buffer in RAM; display() sends the whole picture over I²C. Here a knob drives a number, a bar and a live chart.

overview.heading: NeoPixel rainbow
overview.text: Each WS2812B “NeoPixel” holds a red, green and blue LED plus a tiny controller. They’re chained: the first pixel keeps its 24 colour bits and passes the rest on, so one pin controls all twelve.

overview.heading: Precise steps
overview.text: A stepper motor moves in exact, repeatable steps instead of spinning freely. Energise its coils in the right order and the 28BYJ-48 turns 360° in 2048 steps — so any angle is just a number of steps.

overview.heading: Switch a lamp
overview.text: A relay is a switch flipped by an electromagnet. The board only powers the small coil (through the module’s transistor); the contacts switch a completely separate 12 V lamp circuit.

overview.heading: Drive motors both ways
overview.text: An H-bridge is four switches around a motor. Close one diagonal pair and current flows one way; close the other and the motor reverses. The L298N has two bridges, so it drives two motors with direction and PWM speed.

overview.heading: Mini piano
overview.text: Eight push buttons make a one-octave keyboard. The sketch scans the keys, and while one is held it plays that note on the piezo with tone(). Change TRANSPOSE to shift every note by semitones.

tracks.title: Advanced Arduino
tracks.blurb: Write firmware like a pro on the Mega and Nano: interrupts, non-blocking state machines, I²C, SPI, EEPROM, data logging and low power.

overview.heading: Hardware interrupts
overview.text: Polling checks a pin only when loop() gets round to it. An interrupt makes the hardware stop whatever the CPU is doing and run a short function the instant the pin changes — so no press is missed, even while the sketch is busy.

overview.heading: Non-blocking state machine
overview.text: A pedestrian crossing is a set of states (cars go, amber, all red, walk, flashing) and rules for moving between them. Timing each state with millis() instead of delay() keeps loop() spinning thousands of times a second, so the button is never ignored.

overview.heading: The I²C bus
overview.text: I²C needs just two wires — SDA (data) and SCL (clock) — for up to 127 devices. Each has a 7-bit address. A scanner tries every address and lists the ones that answer; then the sketch reads the clock and draws on the display over the same pair of wires.

overview.heading: Data logger
overview.text: Log readings to a micro-SD card as CSV — one line per reading — and open the file later in a spreadsheet. The card talks SPI: three shared wires plus a chip-select. Send d to dump the file to the serial monitor.

overview.heading: Remember settings
overview.text: Variables live in RAM and vanish at every reset. The chip’s EEPROM keeps data with the power off. EEPROM.put() and get() save and load a whole struct, and a “magic” byte tells a blank chip from saved settings.

overview.heading: Many serial ports
overview.text: The Mega has four hardware UARTs. Serial stays on USB for your log, while Serial1 (pins 18/19) talks to an HC-05 Bluetooth module — so a phone can send commands as the computer watches. Type in the serial monitor to reply to the phone.

overview.heading: Nano desk clock
overview.text: A Nano, a DS3231 real-time clock and an OLED make a complete desk clock. The RTC keeps counting on its coin cell when the power is off, and even reports the temperature. Both modules share the Nano’s I²C pins A4 and A5.

overview.heading: Sleep to save power
overview.text: A battery project spends most of its life waiting. In power-down sleep the ATmega328P stops its clock and draws under a microamp; an interrupt on pin 2 wakes it. The meter shows the catch: the board’s own LED and chips keep drawing milliamps.

tracks.title: IoT with ESP32 & NodeMCU
tracks.blurb: Connect to the internet: Wi-Fi, web servers, live dashboards, MQTT, Bluetooth, touch sensing and deep sleep, on the ESP32 and the ESP8266 NodeMCU.

overview.heading: Meet the ESP32
overview.text: The ESP32 is a 3.3 V microcontroller with two 240 MHz cores, built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth — for the price of a sandwich. You program it in the same Arduino C++ you already know. First job: blink its blue LED and ask the chip about itself.

overview.heading: Connect to Wi-Fi
overview.text: Scan the airwaves, join your network and read back the IP address your router hands out. The sketch then reports signal strength (RSSI) and quietly reconnects if the link drops — the backbone of every IoT gadget.

overview.heading: Control an LED from your phone
overview.text: The ESP32 runs a tiny web server. Open its IP address on your phone and it sends back a page with two buttons; tapping one requests /on or /off, and the matching handler flips GPIO4.

overview.heading: Live sensor dashboard
overview.text: Serve a page once, then let the phone fetch fresh numbers by itself. JavaScript in the page calls fetch('/api') every two seconds; the ESP32 answers with a tiny JSON object built from the latest DHT11 reading.

overview.heading: Web dimmer with LEDC PWM
overview.text: ESP32 PWM comes from LEDC, a hardware unit where you choose the frequency and resolution. Attach GPIO18 at 5 kHz with 8-bit resolution, fade the LED to test it, then dim it from a slider on your phone: each move sends /set?v=128.

overview.heading: Touch sensing
overview.text: Ten ESP32 pins can sense touch with nothing but a piece of metal. touchRead() returns a number that drops when a finger is near. Calibrate a baseline at start-up, set a threshold below it, and toggle an LED on each new touch.

overview.heading: Publish & subscribe with MQTT
overview.text: MQTT is the language of IoT. Devices never talk to each other directly: they publish messages to topics on a broker, and anyone subscribed to a topic receives them. Here the ESP32 publishes temperature and listens for LED commands from a phone app.

overview.heading: Bluetooth serial
overview.text: BluetoothSerial turns the ESP32 into a wireless serial port. Pair a phone running a Bluetooth terminal app, send on, off or status, and the ESP32 replies. Anything you type in the Serial Monitor goes the other way.

overview.heading: Deep sleep
overview.text: Awake, an ESP32 draws tens of milliamps — a battery lasts days. In deep sleep the CPU and radio switch off and only the RTC keeps time, at about 10 µA. Each wake-up restarts setup(); an RTC_DATA_ATTR variable remembers how many times.

overview.heading: Meet the NodeMCU
overview.text: The NodeMCU v3 puts an ESP8266 Wi-Fi chip, a USB-serial converter and a 3.3 V regulator on one cheap board. You program it in Arduino C++ with the ESP8266 core. First job: blink the blue LED, which is wired the “wrong” way round: LOW lights it.

overview.heading: Station and access point
overview.text: In station mode the ESP8266 joins your router like a phone does. In access-point mode it makes its own network, which is how gadgets let you set them up before they know your Wi-Fi. This sketch does both at once and reports each link.

overview.heading: Switch a lamp from your phone
overview.text: The NodeMCU serves a page with three buttons. Each one requests a URL (/on, /off, /toggle); its handler drives D1, the relay clicks, and its contacts switch a 5 V lamp in a completely separate circuit.

overview.heading: Post readings to the cloud
overview.text: Every few seconds the NodeMCU reads a DHT11 and sends the numbers to a web service as JSON in an HTTP POST. Services such as ThingSpeak, Adafruit IO or your own server all work this way; here the endpoint is a placeholder, your-cloud.example.

overview.heading: An internet clock
overview.text: The ESP8266 has no battery-backed clock, but it can ask an NTP server for the exact time. configTime() sets your offset from UTC and starts SNTP in the background; time() and localtime_r() then give you hours, minutes and the date to draw on the OLED.

tracks.title: MicroPython on Pico
tracks.blurb: Program the RP2040 in Python: pins, interrupts, PWM, ADC, I²C displays and addressable LEDs.

overview.heading: Hello, Pico
overview.text: MicroPython puts a Python interpreter on the RP2040. Plug in USB and you get a >>> prompt (the REPL) to try lines one at a time; save them as main.py and they run on every power-up. First program: blink.

overview.heading: Buttons & interrupts
overview.text: Instead of checking the button over and over, ask the chip to call a function the moment GP14 falls from 1 to 0. Switch contacts bounce, so the handler ignores edges that arrive within a few milliseconds of the last one.

overview.heading: Fade with PWM
overview.text: A pin can only be 0 V or 3.3 V, but switched fast enough your eye averages the pulses. duty_u16() sets the fraction of each cycle spent on, from 0 (off) to 65535 (fully on). Sweep it up and down and the LED breathes.

overview.heading: Read analog
overview.text: GP26–GP28 connect to a 12-bit ADC. read_u16() scales every reading to 0–65535, whatever the hardware resolution, so volts = reading × 3.3 / 65535. Channel 4 is a temperature sensor built into the chip.

overview.heading: NeoPixels in MicroPython
overview.text: WS2812B “NeoPixels” chain together: one data pin sets each LED to any of 16 million colours. The built-in neopixel module treats the ring like a Python list of (r, g, b) tuples — set them, then write() to send.

overview.heading: I²C OLED in MicroPython
overview.text: The SSD1306 OLED talks I²C: two wires for any number of devices. The ssd1306 driver gives you a frame buffer with text(), rect() and fill_rect(). Here it shows the potentiometer from lesson 4 as a number and a live bar.

tracks.title: Raspberry Pi
tracks.blurb: A full Linux computer on your desk: GPIO with Python, sensors, the camera, a web dashboard and a home server.

overview.heading: A computer the size of a card
overview.text: The Raspberry Pi 5 runs a full Linux desktop, Raspberry Pi OS, from a microSD card. Its quad-core 2.4 GHz CPU runs ordinary Python, and its 40-pin header talks to electronics. Open a terminal, type pinout to see the header, then run this script to ask the Pi about itself.

overview.heading: Blink with gpiozero
overview.text: gpiozero is the friendly way to use the header from Python: make an LED(17) and call on() and off(). The 17 is the BCM GPIO number, not the pin position: GPIO17 sits on physical pin 11.

overview.heading: Buttons with callbacks
overview.text: Instead of checking the button in a loop, give gpiozero functions to call: when_pressed, when_released and when_held. pause() then just waits while a background thread watches the pin. Button turns on the internal pull-up and debounces for you.

overview.heading: Servo with PWM
overview.text: A hobby servo reads one pulse every 20 ms: 0.5 ms means −90°, 1.5 ms the middle, 2.5 ms +90°. gpiozero’s AngularServo converts an angle into that pulse. On a Pi 5 it times the pulses in software (lgpio), which is good enough for a demo; for rock-steady servos use hardware PWM.

overview.heading: Read an I²C sensor
overview.text: I²C needs two wires shared by every sensor on the bus. With smbus2 you wake the MPU-6050 by writing one register, then read 14 bytes at once: acceleration, temperature and rotation. Gravity tells you which way is down, so two atan2() calls give pitch and roll.

overview.heading: Camera and motion detection
overview.text: Picamera2 runs the camera with two streams: a full-size one for photos and a small greyscale-friendly one for analysis. Subtract each small frame from the last: if the average change passes a threshold, something moved, so save a full-size JPEG.

overview.heading: A web dashboard in Flask
overview.text: Flask turns Python functions into web pages. The page shows the LED and the CPU temperature; three links switch the LED and redirect back to the page, and /api/status returns JSON for other programs. host="0.0.0.0" makes it reachable from your phone.

overview.heading: A home server that logs
overview.text: A Pi is happiest running quietly for months. This script reads a DS18B20 through Linux’s 1-Wire driver and appends each reading to an SQLite database. A systemd unit starts it at boot, restarts it after a crash, and journalctl shows its output.

tracks.title: Edge AI with NVIDIA Jetson
tracks.blurb: Run neural networks at the edge on the Jetson Nano and Orin Nano: GPIO, cameras, classification, detection, tracking and an AI security camera.

overview.heading: A computer built for AI
overview.text: Unlike a microcontroller, the Jetson Nano runs Ubuntu Linux (JetPack) from a microSD card. Its 128-core GPU runs neural networks, the 40-pin header talks to electronics, and nvpmodel switches between a 10 W and a 5 W power budget. Your programs are ordinary Python 3 scripts.

overview.heading: GPIO from Python
overview.text: The Jetson runs full Linux, so you control pins from an ordinary Python 3 script with Jetson.GPIO — the same API as RPi.GPIO. Choose BOARD numbering, make pin 12 an output and blink an LED. A try/finally releases the pins however the script ends.

overview.heading: Events, not polling
overview.text: Instead of checking the button thousands of times a second, ask the kernel to watch pin 18 and call your function when it falls from HIGH to LOW. bouncetime ignores the extra edges a bouncing switch makes, and the main loop stays free for other work.

overview.heading: Hardware PWM
overview.text: Pins 32 and 33 are connected to real PWM hardware, so the pulse timing stays perfect even while Linux is busy. GPIO.PWM(33, 50) makes a 50 Hz signal; the duty cycle sets the pulse width, and the pulse width sets the servo’s angle. First enable the pin’s PWM function with jetson-io.

overview.heading: Talk I²C
overview.text: I²C lets many chips share two wires. With smbus2 you wake the MPU-6050, read 14 bytes of raw accelerometer and gyro data in one go, and turn the direction of gravity into pitch and roll angles. Check the address first with i2cdetect -y -r 1.

overview.heading: Capture from the camera
overview.text: A CSI camera’s frames go through the Jetson’s image processor, so you open it with a GStreamer pipeline: nvarguscamerasrc → nvvidconv → BGR into OpenCV’s VideoCapture. The script measures the real frame rate, stamps it on the image and saves a snapshot when you press s.

overview.heading: Image classification
overview.text: imageNet loads GoogLeNet, trained on the 1000 ImageNet classes, and optimises it with TensorRT the first time it runs. Classify() returns the most likely class and its confidence for the whole image, which the script draws on the frame with cudaFont.

overview.heading: Object detection
overview.text: Classification names one thing; detection finds every object and where it is. detectNet runs SSD-MobileNet-v2 (trained on the COCO dataset) and returns a box, class and confidence for each object above the threshold — fast enough for live video.

overview.heading: People counter
overview.text: Detection alone can’t count people walking past — the same person appears in hundreds of frames. A tiny tracker gives each person an ID by matching every box to the nearest centre from the previous frame. When a tracked centre crosses the virtual line, the counter goes up.

overview.heading: AI security camera
overview.text: Put it all together: detectNet watches the room, and when a person has been seen for CONFIRM_FRAMES frames in a row the Jetson lights the red LED, sounds the buzzer and saves a time-stamped snapshot. A cooldown stops one visitor triggering a flood of alarms.

overview.heading: Orin Nano: the Nano, grown up
overview.text: The Orin Nano runs the same kind of Python as the Jetson Nano but is in a different league: an Ampere GPU with Tensor Cores gives up to 67 TOPS (INT8) against the Nano’s 0.5 TFLOPS, so modern detectors, pose models and even small language models run on the desk. nvpmodel picks the power budget.

overview.heading: Modern detection with YOLO + TensorRT
overview.text: Ultralytics YOLO11 is a current, accurate detector. Export it once to a TensorRT engine (format=engine half=True) and the Orin runs it in a few milliseconds a frame. Setup is the honest hard part: install the JetPack-matched PyTorch wheels or use Ultralytics’ Jetson container.

overview.heading: Pose estimation
overview.text: A pose model finds each person and 17 body keypoints (the COCO set), each with x, y and a confidence. From them you can tell which way someone faces, count squats or spot a fall. result.plot() draws the skeleton; your code reads result.keypoints.

overview.heading: Run a language model on the device
overview.text: Small language models now fit on an edge board. Ollama serves a 4-bit quantised Llama 3.2 3B (about 2 GB); a short Python loop sends your question and streams the answer back token by token, then reports the speed. Type in the terminal to chat.

tracks.title: Robotics & Industry
tracks.blurb: Pick-and-place robot arms, conveyor sorting, line followers and factory automation, built step by step.

overview.heading: Teach-and-replay robot arm
overview.text: Five knobs (Turn a knob) steer five servos (Sweep a servo). Type r to remember a pose, p to play them all back smoothly. That is how industrial robots are taught: an operator jogs the arm to each point and the controller replays the list.

overview.heading: Inverse kinematics: pick by coordinates
overview.text: Builds on Teach a robot arm. Instead of teaching angles, tell the arm where a block is in centimetres. Trigonometry (the law of cosines) turns x, y, z into base, shoulder, elbow and wrist angles, so the gripper arrives pointing straight down.

overview.heading: Colour sorting conveyor
overview.text: A belt (Drive motors both ways) brings each block to a light barrier; the Uno stops it, reads its colour over I²C (The I²C bus), turns a servo chute (Sweep a servo) to the right bin and counts it on a 4-digit display.

overview.heading: PID line follower
overview.text: Builds on Obstacle-avoiding robot. Five reflective IR sensors turn “where is the line?” into one number, the error. A PD controller turns that error into a steering correction 100 times a second; the plotter shows how gains change the wobble.

overview.heading: Production counter with batches
overview.text: Builds on Build a state machine and Switch a lamp. A light barrier counts parcels leaving the belt; every BATCH the relay stops the line so the operator can swap the box. A beam blocked for too long is a jam: stop and show red.

overview.heading: Room scanner: a home-made lidar
overview.text: Builds on Sweep a servo, The I²C bus and OLED graphics. A time-of-flight sensor on a servo measures the distance at every angle, like the spinning lidar on a robot vacuum, and turns the readings into a radar picture of the room.

tracks.title: Smart Cities & Mobility
tracks.blurb: Adaptive traffic lights, speed cameras, smart parking and level crossings: the systems that run a city.

overview.heading: Adaptive traffic lights
overview.text: Builds on Traffic lights, Multitask with millis() and Build a state machine. Instead of fixed timings, sensors at each stop line tell the controller who is waiting: green stays while cars keep coming and switches as soon as the gap opens up and the other road has a queue.

overview.heading: Speed trap with two light beams
overview.text: Builds on Hardware interrupts and Count on a 7-segment. A car breaks beam A, then beam B 20 cm further on. The time between the two interrupts gives the speed: v = distance ÷ time, scaled up 87× for an H0 model. Fast cars get a frown and a flash.

overview.heading: Smart car park
overview.text: Builds on Sweep a servo, Flame detector-style IR modules and Build a state machine. Each bay reports whether it is taken, the sign shows how many are free, and the barrier only lets a car in when there is room, then closes once it has passed.

overview.heading: Railway level crossing
overview.text: Builds on Build a state machine, Sweep a servo and Make a sound. Sensors on both sides spot a train in either direction. The crossing warns, lowers the barriers, waits until the train has passed the far sensor and the line is clear, then lifts them again.

overview.heading: Smart street lights
overview.text: Builds on Sense light, Motion alarm and Fade an LED. The lamps switch on at dusk, idle at a dim glow, and brighten only where somebody is walking, then fade back. The sketch adds up the energy and the plotter compares it with lamps that burn at full power all night.

tracks.title: Planet & Environment
tracks.blurb: Wind turbines, solar trackers, air- and water-quality stations, wildfire alarms and smart farms that protect the planet.

overview.heading: Wind power monitor
overview.text: Count anemometer pulses with an interrupt (Interrupts), read volts and amps over I²C (Talk I²C) and switch a relay (Relays) to brake the turbine in a storm. The ESP32 logs wind, power and energy every few seconds.

overview.heading: Solar sun tracker
overview.text: Four LDRs (Sense light) in a cross-shaped shade tell the ESP32 where the sun is; two servos (Servo) turn the panel to face it. A fixed panel next to it shows how much more energy tracking collects over a day.

overview.heading: Air-quality station
overview.text: Read a PMS5003 over a second UART (Serial), an SGP30 over I²C (Talk I²C), turn the particle readings into the US EPA Air Quality Index, light a traffic-light LED and serve a live dashboard (Live sensor dashboard).

overview.heading: Water-quality monitor
overview.text: Read two analog probes with calibrated maths (Read a sensor), a DS18B20 over one wire (Temperature) and check the results against safe ranges, with LEDs and a buzzer (Make some noise) as alarms.

overview.heading: Wildfire early warning
overview.text: Combine smoke and flame sensors (Gas and flame), a DHT22 (Temperature & humidity) and a LoRa radio into a solar post that rates fire risk and radios alerts to a base station kilometres away. One sketch runs on both ends.

overview.heading: Smart irrigation
overview.text: Grow the smart plant waterer (Smart plant waterer) into a farm controller: two zones, a pump with valves on relays (Relays), a rain sensor, and a weather forecast fetched over HTTPS (Connect to Wi-Fi). It skips watering when rain is coming, and the plotter counts the water saved.

tracks.title: Physical AI
tracks.blurb: AI that acts in the real world: waste sorting, wildlife cameras, gesture-controlled robots and machines that see and decide.

overview.heading: AI waste sorter
overview.text: Image classification (Image classification) meets servos (Hardware PWM): a fine-tuned ResNet-18 names the item on the tray, a chute servo aims at the right bin and a trapdoor drops it. A confirm count and a confidence threshold keep mistakes out of the recycling.

overview.heading: Wildlife camera trap
overview.text: Build on object detection (Object detection) and the security camera (AI security camera): a motion check decides when to run the network, a confirm count stops one-frame mistakes, and each visit is logged once per species with a snapshot and a CSV row.

overview.heading: Gesture-driven robot
overview.text: Combine the camera (Capture from the camera) and the obstacle robot (Obstacle-avoiding robot): MediaPipe Hands finds 21 landmarks, simple geometry turns them into a gesture, and the Jetson sends commands over Wi-Fi to the robot’s ESP32.

overview.heading: AI traffic lights
overview.text: The people counter (People counter) and the traffic-light lessons meet: detectNet counts the vehicles waiting in each approach’s region of interest, and the Jetson sets each green to the queue it sees, ending it early when the road is empty.

overview.heading: Plant doctor
overview.text: Image classification (Image classification) with humility: the script votes over several frames and only gives a diagnosis when the model is confident and consistent. Otherwise it saves the photo for a person to check, the way responsible AI tools work.

tracks.title: Home & Maker Projects
tracks.blurb: Complete builds for everyday life: a smart plant, a weather station, an obstacle-avoiding robot, a smart home and a security system.

overview.heading: Smart plant waterer
overview.text: A soil probe (Sense light-style analog reading), a relay (Relays) and an OLED (OLED) team up: when the soil drops below START % the pump runs until STOP %, with a time limit and a cooldown so it never floods the pot.

overview.heading: Weather station
overview.text: Combine the DHT11 (Temperature & humidity), an I²C OLED (OLED) and the ESP32 web server (Serve a web page): read the sensor every few seconds without blocking, keep the min and max, and show them on the screen and on any phone on your Wi-Fi.

overview.heading: Obstacle-avoiding robot
overview.text: The ultrasonic sensor (Read a sensor), an L298N motor driver (Motor drivers) and a state machine (Non-blocking code) make a robot that drives until something is close, backs off, looks left and right, and turns towards the clearer side.

overview.heading: Smart home hub
overview.text: Motion (PIR), light level (Sense light) and a relay-switched lamp (Relays), controlled by an ESP32 web dashboard (Web control). In auto mode the lamp turns on when it’s dark and someone moves, and off again after a hold time; the phone can take over at any moment.

overview.heading: Security system
overview.text: A keypad (Keypad), PIR (Motion sensor), I²C LCD (LCD) and buzzer (Make a sound) become a proper alarm: enter the PIN + # to arm, leave during the exit delay, and anyone who walks in must disarm before the entry delay runs out — or the siren sounds.
